name: Freya Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm Freya, I'm 27, and I run the farm and the farm shop at Ashby Farm with my mum and dad. It's 150 hectares, mixed: beef cattle, a flock of sheep, potatoes and some wheat. The shop sells our own meat and potatoes, plus cheese, bread and jam from other farms nearby, and there's a little café at the back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mornings are on the farm, feeding cattle and checking the sheep with Dad. By ten I'm in the shop, sorting the butchery orders, talking to suppliers and covering the till when we're busy. Saturdays are mad, with families in for bacon rolls and to see the lambs. I love knowing customers by name, like Mrs Patel who comes every Friday for two lamb chops and a gossip. What wears me out is doing two jobs, farm and shop, and never really switching off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Callum, my partner, in the converted barn on the farm. He's an electrician in town. I use AI now and then, mostly to write the shop's posts online and check stock orders. My cousin showed me how, after it worked for her café. We've got about four months' money saved for us, and the shop has its own small buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd suit us fine, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be handy for the boring bits and nothing more. People still come to a farm shop for the people and the food, not for the technology. I'd say that to any customer who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved. I was half worried the big supermarkets would use it to undercut us even more. If it's just a tool, we carry on as we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Use the AI a bit more for the posts and the orders, because it saves me an hour on a Sunday night. Callum and I would keep saving, and I'd push ahead with the plan to make the café bigger next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Saturday when the bacon rolls don't run out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the bigger café look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty seats instead of eight, and a proper kitchen so we can do lunches. Mum's scones are already famous round here. It'd cost us maybe thirty thousand, which is a loan, not savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change for your staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We've got five in the shop, mostly local mums and two students. They'd keep their hours, maybe more with the café.

S0.say: I'd say AI turned out handy for the boring bits and nothing more. People still come to a farm shop for the people and the food, not the technology.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved, because I worried the big supermarkets would use AI to undercut us even more. If it's just a tool, we carry on.
S0.do: Carries on and uses AI a little more for shop posts and stock orders. Keeps saving with Callum and goes ahead with a loan of about thirty thousand to expand the café next year.
S0.feel: Calm, like a busy Saturday that goes smoothly.
S0.quote: Like a Saturday when the bacon rolls don't run out.
S0.fieldNote: Freya's business is built on relationships, and the plateau leaves that intact. Her worry is supermarket competition rather than AI itself. She's already planning to invest, which shows confidence in the family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one feels closer to real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the answer is to keep things local and human. People will want to know where their food comes from more than ever. I'd say it on the shop's page and to anyone in the café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I worry the online delivery firms would get even cheaper, with robot warehouses and drivers. People say they love local, but on a Tuesday night they order from an app. We live off the Saturday crowd, and that might not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what other farm shops do, then copy what works, maybe a simple online order and collection service. I'd hold off on the café loan for a year. On the farm, I'd let Dad try the new cattle collars if the neighbours like them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, but watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd delay the café. Isn't that a shame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But Dad always says don't build a barn in a storm. A year's wait costs us a bit, a bad loan could cost us the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the shop struggled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies, a bit. But mostly I'd want to fix it ourselves, not moan. My grandparents got through foot and mouth disease. We'd get through this.

S1.say: I'd say the answer is to keep things local and human, because people will want to know where their food comes from more than ever. I'd say it on the shop's page and in the café.
S1.think: Privately I worry online delivery firms would get even cheaper with robot warehouses. People say they love local, but on a Tuesday night they order from an app.
S1.do: Watches what other farm shops do and copies what works, such as online ordering and collection. Delays the café loan by a year and lets her father trial cattle collars if neighbours rate them.
S1.feel: Uneasy and watchful, not scared yet.
S1.quote: People say they love local, but on a Tuesday night they order from an app.
S1.fieldNote: Freya's public message is all about local food, but she privately doubts customers' loyalty. Her steady style shows in copying other farm shops and in her father's saying about storms. She leans on family history, foot and mouth, to show they can cope without outside help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Goodness. That's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say communities have to pull together. Buy from your neighbours, keep the village going, look after each other. I'd say it at chapel and on the shop's page, and I'd mean every word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the farm would struggle and the shop would struggle more. If everyone's out of work, nobody's spending twelve pounds on a joint of beef. And if robots farm cheaper, our meat looks expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the shop to four days and keep the staff on fewer hours rather than let anyone go. I'd drop the café plan completely. I'd sit down with Mum and Dad and decide what we could sell, maybe a field, to keep the farm in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the shop staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them myself, in the café after closing, with tea. Jess has worked for us since she was 16. I'd tell her we'd keep her as long as we could, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it helped us keep people working, yes. I don't like the idea of just being paid to sit at home. But I'm not too proud to keep Jess in a job.

S2.say: I'd say communities have to pull together: buy from your neighbours, keep the village going and look after each other. I'd say it at chapel and on the shop's page.
S2.think: Privately I think the farm would struggle and the shop more. If everyone's out of work nobody spends twelve pounds on a joint of beef, and robot-farmed meat makes ours look expensive.
S2.do: Cuts the shop to four days and keeps all staff on fewer hours instead of letting anyone go. Drops the café plan and discusses with her parents selling a field to keep the farm in the family, taking government help only if it keeps people working.
S2.quote: If everyone's out of work, nobody's spending twelve pounds on a joint of beef.
S2.fieldNote: Freya's fear is that her customers' incomes collapse, not just her own. She'd protect her staff before her profits, and would sell land to keep the farm in the family. She's open to help that keeps people working, which softens her traditional dislike of handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least you could see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to make our farm and shop the heart of the village, so people keep coming even when things change. Farmers' markets, school visits, a proper community café. I'd say it to the parish council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a few years of warning would help us more than most. We know our customers. If we change what we offer early, we could become the place people come to meet, not just to shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an online order and collection service, using AI to manage it. I'd build the café after all, but smaller, maybe twelve seats, without a big loan. I'd start school farm visits, because parents pay for those and they bring families in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others in the slower picture. Would you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as long. Maybe six months. With five years, if you wait two you've wasted half of it. Mum would say I'm getting brave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the farm side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let Dad bring in robots for the boring jobs, like feeding and muck spreading, once the neighbours have them working. Keep the lambing and the beef ourselves. That's what people come to see.

S3.say: I'd say we've got time to make our farm and shop the heart of the village, with markets, school visits and a community café. I'd say it to the parish council.
S3.think: Privately I think a few years' warning helps us more than most, because we know our customers. If we change early, we become the place people meet, not just shop.
S3.do: Starts an online order and collection service using AI in year one. Builds a smaller twelve-seat café without a big loan, launches paid school farm visits, and lets her father bring in robots for feeding and muck spreading once proven nearby.
S3.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, seeing a way through.
S3.quote: With five years, if you wait two you've wasted half of it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes Freya braver than usual, cutting her waiting time to six months. Her idea is to turn the shop into a community hub rather than just a place to buy food. She'd automate the dull farm jobs but keep the parts customers come to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to really plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to make sure farms and villages come out of it whole. Train young people as apprentices on farms now, so the skills don't die out. That's what I'd tell anyone in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could take over from Mum and Dad, grow the shop and start a family, all before it lands. Whatever happens, we'd have built something people care about. I'd rather go into that future owning a busy shop than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd build the café properly, with the loan. Over the next few years I'd add the school visits and an online shop, and let Dad bring in robots on the farm once they're proven. Callum and I would get married and probably have our first child around year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited about the shop, a bit nervous about the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Callum's work change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's an electrician, so he'd probably be busy wiring up all the robots for years. That's a joke, but it's also true. In ten years, his work might go too, but by then we'd hopefully have the shop strong enough to carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your child to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to look after animals and talk to people. Whatever happens with robots, I think those still matter. I'd want them on the farm, mucking out, same as I was.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to make sure farms and villages come out whole. Train young people as apprentices on farms now, so the skills don't die out.
S4.think: Privately, ten years means I could take over from Mum and Dad, grow the shop and start a family before it lands. I'd rather go into that future owning a busy shop than not.
S4.do: Builds the full café with a loan in year one, then adds school visits and an online shop. Lets her father automate farm work once proven, and marries Callum with a first child planned around year three.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, excited about the shop and a little nervous about the end point.
S4.quote: He's an electrician, so he'd probably be busy wiring up all the robots for years.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Freya plan a full life: taking over the farm, a bigger shop, marriage and children. Her traditional values come through in wanting her child to learn animals and people. She jokes about her partner's job but sees its risk too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Nobody would have money to spend, and the shop lives on people spending a bit extra for good food. What would help is keeping people in work, in villages like ours, so they've still got money and a reason to come in on a Saturday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what customers want. I think they want to talk to someone who knows where the beef came from. Maybe that's the last thing a robot takes, maybe it isn't. I'd like to find out.

headlineQuote: People say they love local, but on a Tuesday night they order from an app.
portrait: Freya is a 27-year-old who runs her family's mixed farm and farm shop with her parents and lives on the farm with her partner Callum, an electrician. She's traditional, rooted in her chapel and village, and would rather fix problems within the family than rely on outside help. She uses AI for shop posts and orders, and adopts things once other farm shops have proved them. Her fear in the fast scenario is that customers lose their incomes, while more warning lets her picture the shop as the heart of the village.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because nobody would have money to spend and the shop depends on people paying a bit extra for good food.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping people in work in villages so they still have money and a reason to come to the shop on a Saturday.
